opening.spoken: This record covers the claimed solution of Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness: what has been claimed, what it rests on, and what would have to be checked by whom.

short_version.spoken: On 20 November 2026, the same morning as the Riemann Hypothesis note, Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster posted a 79-page paper and a Lean 4 development in a personal GitHub repository, claiming that smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free initial data on three-dimensional space, and smooth periodic data on the torus, exist for which the Navier–Stokes equations without any force blow up in finite time, at every viscosity. In the Clay formulation this would refute alternatives (A) and (B) and establish (C) and (D) without the force that OpenAI's September claim used. The argument has two parts: a stability result, that one discretely self-similar solution of a certain kind forces blow-up, and the existence of such a solution near an approximate one that satisfies explicit inequalities, which the authors call a certificate. The certificate is not released; the paper gives its hash. That it satisfies the inequalities is checked by interval arithmetic outside the formalization. The authors say the write-up is unpolished and that they posted it rather than wait. Nobody independent has reported building the development or reading the argument. Everything here is open.

cycles.spoken: Tristan Buckmaster posted a statement saying that he and Levent Alpöge had, with large language models, obtained finite-time blow-up with smooth forcing for the incompressible porous media, Boussinesq and three-dimensional Euler equations, crediting the program to Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa; the statement says their Euler proof was checked in Lean on 22 August and that they believed they also had blow-up for hypo-dissipative Navier–Stokes, not yet released. OpenAI announced finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations with a smooth force, with a Lean development; recorded separately as DEBRIEF-math-navierstokes-forced. Buckmaster alleged that OpenAI had adopted the pair's method after learning of their progress; OpenAI denied it. The repository tristanbuckmaster/navier-stokes was created at 10:40 UTC and received its two commits at 13:28 and 13:33 UTC: the paper, dated 20 November and built at 13:22 UTC by its metadata, and the Lean package. Scientific American reported the posting the same day, quoting no independent mathematician. Nervous Machine fetched the paper (sha256 4a01929b…, 1,615,293 bytes) and pinned the repository at its second commit. The Clay Mathematics Institute's problem page lists the problem as Active. DeepMind's formal-conjectures file for the problem, at its latest commit of 29 October, lists (A) and (B) as open and (C) and (D) as solved.

cycles.spoken: The Lean package Alpöge and Buckmaster posted on 20 November builds in full on a machine they have never touched, in twenty-three minutes, with nothing left open in the proof library and nothing beyond Lean's three standard axioms behind any of the nineteen theorems their own comparator files name. The statement files and the solution state those theorems identically. The holes the scan finds are the ones the authors describe: the statement files carry sorry by design, and the solution fills them. What the build shows is narrower than the paper's claim. Every route to blow-up in the package starts from a hypothesis the package does not discharge: a self-similar profile, a certificate, or cell-system data. The certificate the paper names by hash is not in the repository, so nothing here concludes that the Navier–Stokes equations blow up. It concludes that a certificate of the stated form would make them.

findings.spoken: The Lean package released by Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster on 20 November 2026 builds in full at the pinned commit against the pinned Mathlib on a machine the claimants never touched, with no sorry, admit or axiom in its proof library or solution. Each of the nineteen theorems the package's own comparator files name rests on exactly Lean's three standard axioms, and each is stated identically in the statement files and in the solution. Every one of those theorems is an implication whose hypothesis (a self-similar profile, a certificate, or cell-system data) the package does not discharge; the finding says nothing about whether the Navier–Stokes equations blow up.

background.spoken: Do smooth solutions of the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations, started from smooth data, stay smooth for all time, or can the velocity become unbounded in finite time? Fefferman's formulation accepts either answer: a proof of existence and smoothness, with no force on space (A) or on the torus (B), or a proof of breakdown, which may use a smooth force, on space (C) or on the torus (D). A third-party Lean formalization of all four alternatives exists in DeepMind's formal-conjectures; it lists (A) and (B) as open and, since September 2026, (C) and (D) as solved on the strength of OpenAI's forced construction. This claim is the unforced case: it would refute (A) and (B) as stated there.

background.term: The claim by Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster
background.spoken: The paper's abstract says that smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free data on space, and smooth divergence-free data on the torus, exist whose solutions of the unforced three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations blow up in finite time, converging in self-similar variables to a backward discretely self-similar solution and blowing up at its rate. Part one (its Theorem 1.1): a profile, a smooth nonzero solution of the self-similar equations that is periodic in self-similar time up to a linear isometry and has stated decay, implies this blow-up; the proof shows such a solution is stable up to finitely many directions. Part two (its Theorem 7.1): such a profile exists near an approximate one that satisfies explicit inequalities, the certificate. Appendix B describes the certificate's form; Appendix C the computation of the approximate profile. The certificate is not in the repository; the abstract gives its hash and says it will be released soon. That it satisfies the inequalities is checked, the authors say, by interval arithmetic at 128 bits with the Arb library through FLINT, which is not part of the formalization and not in the repository either. The Lean package is the working repository's, with one patch of 20 November applied to the cell-layer statements and dependent proofs, and the README says the patched package was not rebuilt when the repository was assembled. The README also says the formal proofs do not follow the paper's, that the formal statement of the certificate step stops at a weak profile where the paper obtains a smooth one, that the formal definition of a certificate asks more than the paper's in thirteen places, and that the rate and convergence in Theorem 1.1 are not part of the formal statements. The package has no licence file. The authors say in the paper's release that the write-up is unpolished and that after September they could not risk waiting.
